What is Deep Learning? Deep Learning is a subfield of machine learning that uses neural networks with multiple layers to learn representations from data. The layers transform inputs into progressively more useful features for a task. Deep learning is especially useful for images, audio, text, and other complex data. It often benefits from large datasets and substantial computation, although transfer learning can reduce the amount of training required. 2. The artificial neuron An artificial neuron receives input values, multiplies them by weights, adds a bias, and applies an activation function. In simplified form, the computation is y = f(w dot x + b), where x is the input vector, w is the weight vector, b is a bias, and f is an activation function. Common activation functions include ReLU, sigmoid, and tanh. ReLU returns zero for negative inputs and the input itself for positive inputs. Sigmoid maps values into the interval from zero to one and is often used to represent a binary probability. 3. Neural network architecture A feed-forward neural network passes information from an input layer through one or more hidden layers to an output layer. The architecture determines how information is transformed. The output layer depends on the task. A single linear output can be used for regression. A sigmoid output is common for binary classification, while softmax produces a probability distribution over mutually exclusive classes. 4. Loss functions and optimization A loss function measures the difference between model predictions and target values. Mean squared error is commonly used for regression. Cross-entropy loss is widely used for classification. Gradient descent updates model parameters in the direction that reduces the loss. Stochastic gradient descent uses individual or small batches of examples. Adam adapts parameter-specific learning rates using estimates of gradient moments. The learning rate controls the size of parameter updates. A rate that is too high may cause unstable training, while a rate that is too low can make learning very slow.

RAG Research Assistant — Day 1 sample document Page 2 5. Backpropagation Backpropagation applies the chain rule of calculus to compute gradients of the loss with respect to network parameters. The optimizer then uses these gradients to update weights and biases. Training typically repeats a forward pass, loss calculation, backward pass, and optimizer step over many batches and epochs. Monitoring both training and validation loss helps reveal convergence and overfitting. 6. Convolutional and recurrent networks Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) use filters that slide across an input, detecting local patterns such as edges and textures. Pooling or strided convolutions can reduce spatial dimensions. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) process sequences while maintaining a hidden state. Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) networks use gates to manage information over longer sequences. 7. Transfer learning and regularization Transfer learning starts from a model pretrained on a large dataset and adapts it to a target task. A common strategy is to freeze the pretrained feature extractor and train a new classification head, then optionally unfreeze selected layers for fine-tuning. Dropout randomly disables some activations during training. Weight decay penalizes large parameter values. Data augmentation creates varied training examples, and early stopping halts training when validation performance stops improving. 8. Confirm that the loss decreases on a small batch, verify that gradients are nonzero, and ensure the model can overfit a tiny sample as a debugging test. What is Machine Learning? Machine Learning (ML) is a field of artificial intelligence that develops methods allowing computers to learn patterns from data. Instead of writing a separate rule for every situation, a developer provides examples and an algorithm estimates a model that can make predictions on new examples. A machine learning system usually contains data, a representation of that data, a learning algorithm, an objective or loss function, and an evaluation procedure. The quality of the result depends not only on the algorithm but also on the quality and relevance of the data. 2. Main learning paradigms Supervised learning uses examples wi

t depends not only on the algorithm but also on the quality and relevance of the data. 2. Main learning paradigms Supervised learning uses examples with known target labels. Classification predicts categories such as spam or not spam, while regression predicts numerical values such as house prices. Unsupervised learning works with data that has no supplied target labels. Clustering groups similar examples, and dimensionality reduction represents data with fewer variables while attempting to preserve useful structure. Reinforcement learning studies an agent that interacts with an environment. The agent receives rewards or penalties and learns a policy for selecting actions over time. 3. The machine learning workflow A practical workflow begins by defining the problem and selecting an evaluation metric. Next, collect and inspect data, handle missing values, investigate outliers, encode categorical variables, and create useful features. Split the data into training, validation, and test s

e missing values, investigate outliers, encode categorical variables, and create useful features. Split the data into training, validation, and test sets. Fit preprocessing steps only on the training data to avoid data leakage. Use validation data for model selection and reserve the test set for a final, unbiased estimate of performance. Train a baseline model before trying complex methods. Compare alternatives using the same data splits and metric. Finally, inspect errors, document assumptions, and monitor performance after deployment. 4. Common algorithms Linear regression models a numerical target as a weighted combination of input features. Logistic regression estimates class probabilities and is commonly used for binary classification.

RAG Research Assistant — Day 1 sample document Page 2 Decision trees split data into regions using feature-based rules. Random forests combine many trees trained on varied samples and feature subsets, often improving stability. Gradient boosting builds an additive sequence of weak learners, where later learners focus on errors made by earlier learners. Support Vector Machines seek decision boundaries with a large margin between classes. 5. Overfitting and generalization Overfitting occurs when a model captures noise or accidental details in the training set and performs poorly on unseen data. Underfitting occurs when the model is too simple to capture important patterns. Regularization, cross-validation, early stopping, data augmentation, and simpler models can help control overfitting. The goal is generalization: useful performance on examples that were not used to fit the model. 6. Evaluation metrics Accuracy is the fraction of predictions that are correct. Precision measures how many predicted positives are truly positive, while recall measures how many actual positives are found. The F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. For imbalanced classification, accuracy can be misleading. Macro F1 computes an F1 score for each class and averages them equally, giving minority classes meaningful influence. For regression, common metrics include mean absolute error (MAE), mean squared error (MSE), and root mean squared error (RMSE). 7. Data leakage and reproducibility Data leakage happens when information unavailable at prediction time influences training or evaluation. Examples include fitting a scaler on the full dataset before splitting or using future information to predict the past. Why Transformers? Transformers are neural network architectures designed to process sequences using attention mechanisms. Unlike recurrent networks, the standard Transformer can process many token positions in parallel during training. Transformers became central to natural language processing because attention allows each token representation to incorporate information from other relevant tokens in the sequence. 2. Tokenization and embeddings A tokenizer converts raw text into tokens and maps tokens to integer identifiers. Depending on the tokenizer, a token may be a word, part of a word, punctuation, or a special marker. An embedding layer maps token identifie

ntifiers. Depending on the tokenizer, a token may be a word, part of a word, punctuation, or a special marker. An embedding layer maps token identifiers to dense vectors. Since self-attention alone does not encode token order, positional information is added to token representations. Position information may be represented by fixed functions or learned embeddings. 3. Self-attention Self-attention computes relationships between tokens. Each input representation is projected into a query, key, and value vector. Attention scores are computed by comparing queries with keys, scaled, passed through softmax, and used to combine value vectors. The scaled dot-product attention operation is Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QK transpose / sqrt(d_k)) V. The scaling factor helps keep dot products in a useful range as the key dimension grows. Multi-head attention performs several attention operations in parallel. Different heads can learn to focus on different relationships, and their outputs are combin

tention performs several attention operations in parallel. Different heads can learn to focus on different relationships, and their outputs are combined through a learned projection. 4. Encoder and decoder The original Transformer contains an encoder and a decoder. Encoder layers use self-attention and feed-forward networks. Decoder layers use masked self-attention so a position cannot attend to future target tokens, and may also attend to encoder outputs. Encoder-only models such as BERT are commonly used for classification and representation learning. Decoder-only models such as GPT generate text autoregressively. Encoder-decoder models such as T5 are designed for sequence-to-sequence tasks.

RAG Research Assistant — Day 1 sample document Page 2 5. Pretraining objectives Masked language modeling hides selected input tokens and trains a model to predict them from surrounding context. This objective is associated with BERT-style pretraining. Causal language modeling trains a model to predict the next token using only previous context. This objective is commonly used for GPT-style models. Pretraining on large text collections creates general representations that can later be adapted to specific tasks. 6. Fine-tuning and parameter-efficient adaptation Fine-tuning adapts a pretrained model to a downstream dataset. A classification task may add a task-specific output head and train it with labeled examples. Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods update only a small subset of parameters or add small trainable modules. During fine-tuning, use a validation set for model selection, monitor overfitting, and keep the test set separate until final evaluation. 7. Practical considerations Choose a tokenizer that matches the pretrained model. Truncation and padding control sequence length, while attention masks indicate which positions are real tokens rather than padding. Batch size, learning rate, maximum sequence length, warmup, weight decay, and number of epochs all influence training. Start with a small baseline and change one major factor at a time. Generation settings such as maximum new tokens, temperature, and top-p affect output behavior. They should be selected based on the application rather than treated as universal defaults. 8. Context length: the maximum sequence length a model can process in one input. Checkpoint: saved model parameters and configuration. Fine-tuning: adapting pretrained parameters to a target task.
